content.title: About
content.content: Kimchi is a traditional Korean dish of fermented vegetables, most commonly napa cabbage, radish, carrot and a blend of spices. It has a spicy, slightly sour flavor and aromas of garlic, ginger and fish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kimchi is considered Korea’s national dish and is eaten daily by more than 90 % of the population.
Traditional fermentation can last from a few days to several months, depending on temperature.
There are over 200 varieties of kimchi, differing in vegetables and spice mixes.
Kimchi is often served as a side dish but is also used in soups, stir‑fries and pancakes.
In 2013 UNESCO inscribed kimchi on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Fermentation makes kimchi rich in live lactobacilli, which support gut health.

items.title: Vitamins B and C
items.content: The vegetables and spices provide vitamin C and B‑vitamins (B1, B2, B6) important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Garlic, ginger and red pepper contain antioxidant compounds.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Probiotics and vitamins together may enhance the immune response.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Kimchi is low in calories while delivering strong flavor.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Kimchi is often prepared with a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes include fish sauce; those with allergies should choose vegetarian versions.

items.title: Fermentation gas
items.content: Some people may experience bloating from excessive fermented foods.

items.title: Quality control
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of unwanted bacteria; always respect shelf‑life dates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kimchi is served as a side dish, added to soups (e.g., kimchi‑jjigae), rice dishes, pancakes and salads. It can be eaten fresh after fermentation or aged for a stronger flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store kimchi in an airtight glass jar in the refrigerator. When kept properly it remains good for weeks to months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or mold.
